title: DeepPrim: Physics-Driven 3D Weather Forecasting
one_liner: A weather forecaster that learns the actual physics equations governing the atmosphere instead of just memorizing patterns.
lead: Weather forecasting is hard because the atmosphere is complicated — countless gases, temperature, moisture, and wind all interacting. Traditional forecasts use simplified physics (numerical weather prediction, or NWP) that skip hard details to run fast, while modern AI models usually ignore the physics entirely and just learn from data. DeepPrim does something different: it teaches a neural network to actually learn and solve the primitive equations — the core physics that describes how air moves and weather forms — instead of memorizing patterns or faking physics.

problem.h2: Why old forecasts miss the weather
paras: Weather happens because gas, heat, and water vapor follow the laws of physics. But solving those laws perfectly is too slow — checking every tiny patch of air every second would take weeks to forecast tomorrow. So meteorologists use a shortcut: they solve the simplified laws on a coarse grid (maybe one square kilometer per point) and skip hard details they assume don't matter much. This works okay, but it misses storms, shifts rain timing, and fails when conditions are weird.

A beginner might try: 'Just train a neural network on past weather and recent conditions — it will learn the real patterns.' But that pure learning approach has a problem — the network learns surface correlations (when humidity is high, rain often follows) but does not learn the actual mechanism (air rises, cools, water condenses). When conditions are new or extreme, the network guesses wrong because it never learned the rules, just the most common stories.
So the real problem is: we can either use simplified physics (fast but incomplete) or pure pattern learning (flexible but unreliable), but we cannot easily have both.

callout.html: DeepPrim teaches a neural network to learn and solve the actual physical equations that govern how the atmosphere moves.

steps.text: Temperature, wind, humidity at many heights above ground.
It learns to compute the primitive equations: how air accelerates, how temperatures change, how moisture moves.
Not a direct forecast, but the rate of change (how much wind will shift, how much temperature will rise, how humidity evolves).
Add those changes to the current state to get the next hour or day.
Run the network again on the new state to forecast the next step.

paras: Instead of having the network directly guess 'what will the weather be in 6 hours', DeepPrim makes it learn to compute the rates of change — how much each quantity (wind, temperature, humidity) shifts each hour — by solving the actual differential equations that physicists write down. The network becomes an equation solver, not a pattern memorizer, because solving equations is more reliable when conditions are new.

hidden.name: How well the learned equations conserve physics
paras: The paper measures whether the network's learned equations obey conservation laws — rules that say certain quantities (like total mass, total energy) cannot be created or destroyed. For example, if air rises in one place, it must descend elsewhere; if the atmosphere heats up in one region, it must cool elsewhere. A pure AI model can violate these rules everywhere; the physics-trained network respects them.

The paper estimates this by checking: after the network predicts, do the conservation laws still hold? Do the predicted wind patterns conserve mass? Do the energy equations balance? When they do, the forecast stays realistic even far into the future.

heat.caption: Darker means more important conservation laws the network must respect. Highlighted ones are checked hardest.

reads.html: Physical consistency means the predicted weather still obeys the laws that real weather obeys — air cannot appear out of nothing, energy must flow logically, and patterns must follow the rules of motion and heat.

The network learns a physics-informed neural network (PINN) architecture where layers encode the primitive equations (Navier-Stokes in pressure coordinates, the thermodynamic equation, the continuity equation for water vapor). The loss function includes both data fidelity and a physical constraint term that penalizes violations of conservation laws.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: teaching physics beats pure pattern learning
paras: A pure neural network trained only on 'input conditions -> output weather' learns to recognize common patterns, but it has no reason to respect physical laws. It might predict wind shifts that violate conservation of mass or temperature changes that break energy balance. In rare or extreme situations where the training examples do not cover the case, the network fails catastrophically because it never learned the actual rules.

DeepPrim embeds the primitive equations into the network's structure. Each layer of the network performs a piece of the physics calculation — computing how pressure changes drive wind, how wind advects temperature, how water vapor condenses. Now the network cannot output nonsensical predictions because its own design forbids it. When conditions change dramatically, the network still respects the laws, so its forecast stays plausible.

The mechanism is this: by teaching the network to solve equations instead of memorize examples, the network learns the deep structure of weather dynamics. It can extrapolate to new situations because it learned the rules, not just the patterns. Physics acts like a strong constraint that forces the network to learn only what is real and necessary, filtering out spurious correlations that look good in data but do not exist in nature.

stages.s: Recent weather: wind, temperature, humidity at each height
Layer 1: Compute pressure-gradient force (Navier-Stokes momentum equation)
Layer 2: Compute how wind advects temperature (transport equation)
Layer 3: Compute how water vapor condenses (thermodynamic feedback)
Layer 4: Integrate rates to get new state
Next forecast: wind, temperature, humidity one time step ahead

math.h2: The core equation: solving primitive equations
math.words: The rate of change of wind equals the pressure gradient force plus the Coriolis force; the rate of change of temperature equals the heat from rising air and solar input; the rate of change of humidity equals the transport of water vapor minus losses to condensation. The network learns the coefficients and feedbacks in these three coupled equations.
math.equation: du/dt = -(1/rho) * dP/dx + f*v + F_wind; dT/dt = -u*dT/dx - (omega/Cp)*dT/dp + Q; dq/dt = -u*dq/dx + E - C
symbols: wind speed in the x direction (east-west)
how fast the wind changes each hour
air density (how tightly packed the air is)
how pressure changes over distance (the pressure gradient)
wind speed in the y direction (north-south)
how fast temperature changes each hour
vertical pressure velocity (how fast air rises or falls)
heat capacity of air at constant pressure
water vapor mixing ratio (how much water is in the air)
condensation that forms clouds and rain

worked.title: A tiny worked example: how wind changes in one place
lines: Suppose pressure drops 1 unit over 100 km distance to the east, air density is 1.2 kg/m^3, and the Coriolis factor (Earth's rotation effect) is f = 0.0001.
Pressure gradient force: dP/dx = 1/100 = 0.01 units/km; (1/rho)*dP/dx = 0.01/1.2 = 0.0083 m/s per hour.
If no other forces, wind accelerates eastward by 0.0083 m/s each hour.
But Coriolis force also acts (Earth rotation turns moving objects): f*v term adds 0.0001 * (current northwind speed).
The network learns both terms and combines them to predict how the wind field evolves realistically over 24 hours.

math.note: The network does not just memorize these equations; it learns to compute them faithfully given data, so new conditions still produce physically consistent forecasts.

charts.title: Simplified traditional NWP (skips hard details)
charts.note: Loses accuracy fast because it missed early signs of unresolved processes.

charts.title: DeepPrim (learns the equations)
charts.note: Stays accurate longer because it learned the actual physics, so it captures the buildup of storms and rare conditions.

items.b: If the training data is biased (missing rare storms or very cold days).
items.html: The network learns correct equations only for the situations it saw. A heatwave or freak snowstorm outside the training envelope will still baffle it, because the equations are learned from data.

items.b: If the network is too small to express the full equations.
items.html: The primitive equations are three-dimensional, coupled, and nonlinear. If the network is not deep or wide enough (not enough neuron layers or neurons per layer), it cannot learn all the feedback loops, and the forecast drifts off reality fast.

items.b: If the pressure coordinate system is wrong.
items.html: The network is trained to solve equations in pressure coordinates (a vertical grid based on air pressure, not altitude). If the pressure coordinate is not set up right, the network's equations do not match reality.

If the network is large enough, trained on diverse weather (common and extreme), and the pressure coordinates are set correctly, the learned equations become trustworthy even on new conditions — because it learned the laws, not just the patterns.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A good demo would train DeepPrim on historical weather data (say, 10 years of global observations), then test it on a year it never saw. Compare: (1) the traditional simplified NWP forecast (from official weather services), (2) a pure neural network baseline (trained on the same data but with no physics constraints), and (3) DeepPrim. Measure accuracy as mean absolute error in temperature, wind speed, and precipitation at each forecast lead time (6 hours, 12 hours, 24 hours, 3 days, 5 days). The point is to show that DeepPrim stays accurate longer than the baseline, especially on extreme events (storms, heat waves) that the pure neural network got wrong.
demo.metric_eq: accuracy = 100 * (1 - mean_absolute_error / typical_weather_variance); for each lead time, compare traditional NWP vs. pure NN baseline vs. DeepPrim
demo.closing: The demo should make it impossible to miss this: DeepPrim forecasts stay physically plausible and accurate even far into the future and even for rare weather events, while a pure neural network drifts off into nonsense because it never learned the actual rules.
